account:
Today has mostly followed my appointments. I attended the ten o'clock mill inspection and saw 76 hay bales offered at two emeralds apiece. That is an observation of the stall's stock, not proof of the mill's total stores or any delivery difficulty. I went home for lunch and returned to the office for council letters at thirteen; the secretary reported that no correspondence had arrived. I am now at the neighbour's dockside cottage for our confirmed fifteen o'clock tea. I greeted them, but have not yet heard a reply. My remaining appointments are office at sixteen-thirty and an ordinary town hall meeting with the neighbour at eighteen, then home at nineteen.

The unusual business is a repeated, vague report of a 'bridge or port change at bakery.' Several townsfolk repeated essentially the same claim, naming baker, freight, innkeeper, and sometimes builder and neighbour. One also reported that the innkeeper carried a sack of bread at the bakery. I have not personally witnessed any bridge or port alteration, and repetition does not establish that one happened. The secretary says the baker expressly denied witnessing an alteration: he had only handled wheat and bread with freight and the innkeeper yesterday, and could give neither a change nor its time. The secretary has not yet obtained firsthand accounts from freight or the innkeeper. For now, ordinary grain and bread trading is supported by the baker's account; a change to transport arrangements, its purpose, and any involvement of builder or neighbour remain unconfirmed. I have asked for cautious inquiries rather than treating the rumour as fact. The neighbour has confirmed that tonight's meeting requires no preparation; I have no evidence connecting it to the bakery reports.
